name: Neopalatial Knossos at its height
summary: The rebuilt palace at Knossos is the largest Minoan centre, with frescoes, storerooms and shrines. Its religion — goddess figures, bull-leaping, peak sanctuaries — is visible in images but cannot be read.
uncertainty: Minoan Linear A is undeciphered, so Minoan god names are unknown. Links to later Greek myth (Minos, the Labyrinth) are interpretations, not attestations.

name: Linear B archive at Knossos
summary: Clay tablets in Linear B — an early form of Greek — record offerings to deities, including 'a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja' (Mistress of Atana) and 'e-ri-nu' (Erinys).
uncertainty: The date of the destruction that baked the Knossos tablets is disputed; some scholars place it considerably later. The reading of 'Atana' as Athena is probable but not certain.

name: Mycenae's Lion Gate and citadel walls
summary: The fortified citadel of Mycenae, with its Cyclopean walls and Lion Gate, is the archetypal Mycenaean palace centre — the place later poets made Agamemnon's capital.
uncertainty: No text from the site names a king Agamemnon. The association is a later poetic one.

name: Linear B tablets at Pylos name the gods
summary: Tablets baked in the fire that destroyed the Palace of Nestor record offerings to Zeus (di-we), Hera (e-ra), Hermes (e-ma-a2), Poseidon (po-se-da-o) and Dionysus (di-wo-nu-so-jo), among others.
uncertainty: The tablets give names and offerings, not myths. That these gods had the same stories or roles as in Homer cannot be assumed.

name: Destruction layers at Hisarlik (Troy VI–VIIa)
summary: The Bronze Age city at Hisarlik in north-west Anatolia was damaged (Troy VIh) and later destroyed by fire with signs of conflict (Troy VIIa). Hittite texts mention a city called Wilusa, widely identified with (W)ilios.
uncertainty: Archaeology shows a destroyed Late Bronze Age city. It does not show who destroyed it, or that the Iliad's war happened. Earthquake, raiding and wider collapse are all proposed causes.

name: Collapse of the Mycenaean palaces
summary: Across the eastern Mediterranean, palace systems fall. In Greece Linear B writing disappears and will not be replaced for several centuries.
uncertainty: Causes are debated: drought, earthquakes, systems failure, migration and raiding (the 'Sea Peoples') probably combined.

name: The Lefkandi 'heroon' burial
summary: On Euboea, a man and a woman are buried with horses and rich imports beneath a monumental apsidal building, showing elite wealth and Near Eastern contact in the supposed 'Dark Age'.
uncertainty: Whether the building was a hero-shrine, a house or a funerary monument is debated.

name: Earliest offerings at Olympia
summary: Bronze and terracotta figurines, many of animals, begin to accumulate in the Altis at Olympia, the start of a sanctuary that would become Zeus' greatest.
uncertainty: Continuity of cult from the Bronze Age is not established; the earliest offerings cannot be tied to Zeus by inscription.

name: Greeks adopt the alphabet
summary: Greeks adapt the Phoenician script, adding vowels. The earliest inscriptions follow soon after — making it possible, eventually, to write down the oral epics.
uncertainty: The exact date and place of adoption are debated; some argue for an earlier transfer.

name: Traditional date of the first Olympic Games
summary: Later Greek chronographers counted the Olympiads from this year, when Koroibos of Elis was said to have won the footrace.
uncertainty: The date comes from a victor list compiled centuries later (attributed to Hippias of Elis). Archaeology suggests organised games began somewhat later.

name: Apollo's sanctuary at Delphi takes shape
summary: Votive offerings increase sharply at Delphi, and the oracle becomes consulted across the Greek world, notably for founding colonies.
uncertainty: Claims of a Bronze Age oracle of Earth or Themis come from later myth and drama, not from archaeological evidence of continuity.

name: Composition of the Iliad and Odyssey
summary: The two epics reach something like their surviving form, the product of a long oral tradition. They are the oldest surviving Greek literature.
uncertainty: Dating Homer is contested: proposals range from earlier to considerably later, and a fixed written text may come later still (e.g. the Athenian 'Peisistratean recension').

name: Hesiod composes the Theogony
summary: A Boeotian poet sets out the generations of the gods from Chaos to Zeus, the earliest surviving systematic account of Greek theogony.
uncertainty: Relative dating against Homer is debated; West placed Hesiod's Theogony before the Homeric epics. The ending of the poem was probably extended by later hands.

name: Homeric Hymn to Apollo
summary: A hymn in epic style narrates Apollo's birth on Delos and his foundation of the oracle at Pytho.
uncertainty: The hymn may join a Delian and a Pythian poem of different dates; one ancient tradition links its performance to Polycrates' festival on Delos.

name: Homeric Hymn to Demeter
summary: The fullest early account of Persephone's abduction and the founding of Demeter's Mysteries at Eleusis.
uncertainty: Linguistic dating places it in the Archaic period, but the range is wide.

name: Archaic Telesterion at Eleusis
summary: Successive initiation halls are built for Demeter's Mysteries, enlarged under the Peisistratids — material evidence of the cult the Hymn describes.
uncertainty: Earlier phases, including a possible Mycenaean building under the hall, are of debated religious function.

name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitol
summary: Roman tradition dates the dedication of the great temple of the Capitoline triad — Jupiter, Juno and Minerva — to the first year of the Republic.
uncertainty: The date is Roman tradition (Livy); the temple's massive foundations survive, but the precise year is not independently confirmed.

name: The Parthenon is built
summary: Athens builds a marble temple for Athena Parthenos; its sculptures show her birth and her contest with Poseidon on the pediments.
uncertainty: Building dates are secured by surviving inscribed building accounts; interpretations of the frieze remain debated.

name: Herodotus on who 'made' the gods' genealogies
summary: Herodotus writes that Homer and Hesiod gave the Greeks the gods' genealogies, names, honours and forms — an ancient recognition that poets shaped the pantheon.

name: Alexander consults Zeus-Ammon at Siwa
summary: Alexander travels to the Egyptian oracle of Amun, whom Greeks called Zeus Ammon, an emblem of the Greek-Egyptian religious blending of the age that followed.
uncertainty: What the oracle told Alexander was later embellished; our main accounts were written centuries afterwards from earlier sources.

name: Cult of Sarapis in Ptolemaic Alexandria
summary: The early Ptolemies promote Sarapis, a god combining Egyptian Osiris-Apis with features of Zeus, Hades and Asclepius, with a great Serapeum at Alexandria.
uncertainty: How deliberately the cult was 'designed' by the Ptolemies is debated.

name: Rome's lectisternium of twelve gods
summary: During the war with Hannibal, Rome sets out couches for twelve gods in six pairs — Jupiter with Juno, Neptune with Minerva, and so on — a set modelled on the Greek Twelve.

name: Ovid's Metamorphoses
summary: A Latin epic of transformations retells hundreds of Greek myths under Roman names, shaping how later Europe knew them.

name: The Bibliotheca of 'Apollodorus'
summary: A prose handbook systematically summarises Greek myth from the gods' origins to the heroes' returns, drawing on many lost earlier works.
uncertainty: Wrongly attributed to Apollodorus of Athens; the real author and date are unknown.

name: Pausanias tours the sanctuaries
summary: A Greek traveller describes the sanctuaries, cults and local myths of Greece under Roman rule — invaluable for Olympia, Delphi and Eleusis.

name: Theodosian edicts against sacrifice
summary: Imperial laws forbid sacrifice and visits to temples. Public worship of the Olympian gods loses legal standing, though myth lives on in literature and education.
uncertainty: Enforcement varied widely by region; the laws did not end all traditional worship at once.
